PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 55 — Lesson 79: Preventive Care & Screening Assessment

FNP-level goal: Build an individualized prevention plan from age, anatomy, exposures, family history, pregnancy status, medical conditions, medications, health behaviors, social context, and patient goals. Distinguish screening from diagnostic evaluation, communicate benefits and harms honestly, use shared decision-making where appropriate, and never let a normal screening result delay workup of a concerning symptom.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary prevention in FNP practice.
  • Distinguish population screening from diagnostic evaluation of a symptomatic patient.
  • Explain false-positive, false-negative, overdiagnosis, incidental findings, and downstream-procedure risks in plain language.
  • Construct a prevention plan that includes vaccines, cancer screening, cardiometabolic risk, infection/STI prevention, reproductive health, mental health, substance use, injury prevention, oral/vision/hearing care, and social needs.
  • Use current guidelines rather than memory for exact ages, intervals, products, contraindications, and risk criteria.
  • Document informed/shared decisions, declined services, follow-up ownership, and a safe diagnostic path for symptoms.

Part 1 — Prevention Has Levels and Purposes

Primary prevention aims to prevent disease before it occurs: immunization, tobacco cessation, physical activity, nutrition, injury prevention, safer-sex counseling, and risk-reduction treatment when indicated. Secondary prevention identifies disease early through appropriate screening. Tertiary prevention reduces complications and disability after disease is established: diabetes kidney/eye/foot surveillance, cardiac rehabilitation, medication adherence, and fall prevention are examples.

Quaternary prevention protects patients from unnecessary testing, labeling, procedures, and treatment harm. It asks: “Will this service improve outcomes for this patient, or could it start a cascade with more harm than benefit?” High-quality prevention is not an indiscriminate checklist; it is evidence-based, individualized, feasible, and aligned with patient values.

Part 2 — Screening Is Not Diagnosis

Screening is performed in people without symptoms to identify those who may benefit from additional evaluation. A screening test does not usually diagnose disease. An abnormal screen leads to a diagnostic pathway, while a normal screen lowers risk only within the limits of that test. Cancer, cardiovascular, infectious, mental-health, and other screenings must be selected for the patient’s risk, age, anatomy, condition, life expectancy, and the availability of effective follow-up.

A symptom changes the question. New breast mass, rectal bleeding, hematuria, postmenopausal bleeding, persistent cough, unexplained weight loss, changing mole, chest pain, or focal neurologic deficit is not “screening,” even if the patient had a normal screening result previously. Evaluate concerning symptoms diagnostically and promptly. Do not reassure a symptomatic patient solely because their screening is up to date.

Part 3 — Benefits, Harms, and Uncertainty

Before recommending a preventive service, explain what condition it looks for, who is most likely to benefit, what the test/procedure involves, possible false-positive and false-negative results, potential downstream testing, overdiagnosis, treatment burden, and what happens after each possible result. A false-positive can create anxiety and invasive testing; a false-negative can delay recognition when symptoms occur. Some tests identify conditions that would never have become clinically important, yet may lead to treatment harms.

Use absolute, plain-language communication whenever possible. Avoid saying “this test prevents cancer” when it may instead lower risk or detect disease earlier in certain groups. Ask the patient to explain the plan back in their own words. Informed consent is not a signature; it is an understanding of benefits, harms, alternatives, uncertainty, and next steps.

Part 4 — Build a Risk Profile Before Opening the Checklist

Start with age, sex assigned at birth/anatomy as clinically relevant, gender identity/pronouns, pregnancy possibility, family history and age at diagnosis, personal cancer history, genetic results when available, tobacco/nicotine exposure, alcohol and other substances, occupation/environment, sexual practices, travel, housing, food access, violence risk, chronic conditions, immune status, medications, and prior screening/vaccine records. Avoid assumptions from appearance, race/ethnicity, relationship status, or a problem list.

Risk is dynamic. New immune suppression, pregnancy, a new family-history detail, a medication change, renal disease, previous abnormal screening, or a change in sexual practices can modify a preventive plan. The EHR gap list is a prompt, not a final decision. Verify source records and current national/local guidance before ordering or deferring a service.

Part 5 — Immunization Assessment at Every Encounter

Assess immunization status at every clinical encounter, reconcile documented doses with the current schedule, and identify routine, catch-up, risk-based, travel/occupational, and shared-clinical-decision recommendations. Determine contraindications and precautions from the patient’s history and current condition; do not invent a contraindication because of an unrelated fear or mild prior symptom without reviewing current guidance.

Exact schedules, products, intervals, and recommendations change. Use the current CDC schedule and clinical notes rather than memorizing a static table. Explain expected common reactions, serious warning symptoms, and how the patient will receive/document the vaccine. If vaccination is declined, explore the reason respectfully, give evidence-based information, document the discussion, and leave the door open for a future decision.

Part 6 — Cancer Screening: Individualize and Close the Loop

Appropriate cancer screening depends on the organ at risk, age, risk factors, prior results, medical history, functional status, life expectancy, and patient preferences. Review screening history carefully: test type, date, result, adequacy, recommended interval, and whether abnormal findings completed their diagnostic pathway. “Patient says normal” is not always enough when a result or pathology report is available.

Abnormal screening requires ownership. Define who contacts the patient, orders diagnostic testing, tracks completion, interprets results, coordinates specialty care, and communicates the next step. Lost-to-follow-up abnormal results are a preventable diagnostic-safety failure. Patients with symptoms require diagnostic evaluation even if screening was recently normal.

Part 7 — Cardiometabolic Prevention Is More Than a Lab Panel

Assess blood pressure with correct technique and repeat/confirm abnormal results as appropriate. Review weight trajectory, waist/central adiposity when useful, activity, nutrition, sleep, tobacco/nicotine, alcohol, glucose status, lipid history, kidney disease, family history, pregnancy complications, and social constraints. Integrate cardiovascular risk with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory disease, mental health, medications, and patient goals.

Preventive counseling succeeds when it is specific and feasible. “Eat better and exercise” is not a plan for a patient with food insecurity, chronic pain, unsafe neighborhood, shift work, caregiving duties, depression, or no time for appointments. Use small achievable changes, referrals/community resources, medication and monitoring plans when indicated, and follow-up that tests whether the plan works for the actual patient.

Part 8 — Sexual, Reproductive, and Infectious Prevention

Use an inclusive sexual history to determine STI/HIV/hepatitis testing and prevention needs without stigma. Ask about anatomic sites of exposure, partners, barrier use, pregnancy intention, contraception, prior testing/infections, coercion/safety, and access to confidential care. Screening frequency and prevention choices should reflect current guidance and the patient’s exposures—not identity labels alone.

Review reproductive life planning, medication safety in pregnancy, cervical/other anatomy-based prevention, immunizations, fertility goals, and postpartum needs where relevant. Discuss infection prevention, testing, vaccines, and treatment linkage in a way that supports autonomy and privacy. A patient with symptoms still needs diagnostic evaluation; prevention screening is not a substitute for examining dysuria, discharge, lesions, pelvic pain, testicular pain, or systemic illness.

Part 9 — Behavioral, Injury, and Social Prevention

Prevention includes depression/suicide risk, substance use, sleep, intimate-partner/elder/child safety, firearm and medication safety where relevant, falls, driving, hearing, vision, oral health, nutrition, physical activity, and social determinants. Ask permission and normalize the questions: “I ask all patients because these issues affect health and safety.” Respond to positive findings with a concrete pathway, not a checkbox alone.

Screening for a condition without access to follow-up can create harm. Before ordering, consider language, transportation, insurance, cost, disability accommodations, caregiver support, digital access, and local services. Connect patients with care navigation, social work, public-health programs, or community resources when those barriers determine whether prevention is possible.

Part 10 — Shared Decision-Making and Prioritization

Some preventive choices are routine for an eligible patient; others require individualized shared clinical decision-making because benefits, harms, uncertainty, or preferences vary. A shared decision includes the patient’s understanding of the condition and service, benefits/harms/alternatives/uncertainty, their values, and a jointly chosen plan. The patient’s desired degree of involvement may vary.

Do not attempt every preventive conversation in one visit. Prioritize acute safety first, then high-impact gaps and what matters most to the patient. Arrange follow-up for deferred items. A thoughtful plan that the patient can complete is safer than an exhaustive list that overwhelms them and results in no action.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Normal Screen, New Symptom

A 59-year-old had a normal screening test last year but now has progressive rectal bleeding, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss.

FNP reasoning: this is a diagnostic presentation, not a screening reminder. Assess stability and anemia/bleeding risk, build the differential, and arrange the appropriate diagnostic pathway. Prior normal screening does not explain current red flags.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: A “Declined” Vaccine

A patient says they “do not do vaccines” because of a prior episode of fever and soreness after an injection. They have no history suggesting a serious allergic reaction.

FNP reasoning: clarify the experience, check current recommendations/contraindications, discuss expected effects and benefits/harms respectfully, address questions, and document the decision. Do not shame the patient or incorrectly label an ordinary reaction as a contraindication.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Competing Priorities

A 46-year-old with uncontrolled hypertension, tobacco use, depression, food insecurity, and several overdue preventive services arrives for a brief visit.

FNP reasoning: assess urgent symptoms and safety first; then prioritize the highest-impact, feasible next step with the patient. Link blood-pressure care, tobacco support, mood/safety assessment, food resources, and scheduled follow-up rather than delivering an unusable list of ten tasks.

FNP Preventive-Care Framework

  1. Stabilize symptoms first: distinguish screening from a diagnostic presentation every time.
  2. Build an updated risk profile: anatomy, age, family/personal history, exposures, conditions, medicines, immune status, and social context.
  3. Check current evidence: use current guideline sources for intervals, eligibility, products, contraindications, and risk thresholds.
  4. Explain benefits and harms: false positives/negatives, downstream tests, overdiagnosis, procedure risk, and uncertainty.
  5. Use shared decisions: explore the patient’s goals, understanding, concerns, preferred role, and feasibility.
  6. Close the loop: track abnormal results, diagnostic completion, referrals, immunization documentation, and preventive follow-up.
  7. Address access: make the plan achievable through navigation, language support, cost/transport solutions, and community linkage.

High-Yield Summary

Screening: is for asymptomatic populations and generally identifies who needs diagnostic evaluation; it is not a diagnosis.
Symptoms: require diagnostic thinking even after a normal screening result.
Prevention: includes immunization, cancer/cardiometabolic/infection prevention, behavioral health, injury prevention, and social supports.
Harms: false positives, false negatives, downstream procedures, overdiagnosis, and access burden are part of informed care.
Guidelines: change; verify current recommendations rather than relying on memory.
Shared decision: means evidence plus patient values, understanding, alternatives, uncertainty, and a jointly chosen plan.
FNP standard: prioritize, personalize, document, and close the loop.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Screening, immunization, preventive medication, genetic testing, referral, and follow-up decisions must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation. New or concerning symptoms require clinical diagnostic evaluation, not an app-based screening interpretation.
